corrected_value.title: The influence of personal BMI on body size estimations ans sensitivity to body size change in anorexia spectrum disorders

decisions.quote: Statistically, the central finding of Cornelissen et al. [17] that supports a difference in the way healthy controls and women with ANSD perceive body size was a significant interaction between BMI and participant group in predicting self-estimated body size. In this replication study, we followed the same design as Cornelissen et al. [17] by comparing ~100 healthy controls to ~30 women with ANSD, maintaining a sample size ratio of ~ 3:1.

decisions.reason: The shipped original (Cornelissen et al., 2016, 10.1111/bjhp.12185, Ref [20]) is only cited inside the background range [19-25] for normal contraction bias in healthy individuals (lines 5 and 110) and is not re-tested as the target of this eating-disorder vs control replication. Instead, the study explicitly states that it serves as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17, 18] (line 25) and directly follows the design and power parameters of Cornelissen et al. [17] (2015, 10.1016/j.bodyim.2015.01.001, blind target 0), making blind_right the correct replacement for row 1858.

decisions.quote: When analysing the entire clinical group, their self-estimated BMI closely matched their actual BMI, evidenced by a regression slope close to one (see Fig 2), suggesting a relatively accurate perception of own body size across the actual BMI range. However, excluding the participants with a history of bulimia nervosa and repeating the analysis, yielded results more consistent with Cornelissen et al. [17,18], as illustrated in Fig 3. Specifically, the regression slope of estimated BMI on actual BMI had a slope > 1, with accurate estimation at low actual BMI, and systematically increasing overestimation as actual BMI increased. How should we reconcile these differences in the results? We argue that our most important finding is that both multivariate analyses revealed a statistically significant interaction between participant group and actual BMI, irrespective of the inclusion or exclusion of participants with a history of bulimia nervosa.
decisions.location: Discussion > Participants with a history of ED, line 115
decisions.reason: Evaluating outcome for the resolved target Cornelissen et al. (2015) [17] (as well as [18], which shares the identical comparisons): the authors confirm replication of the actual BMI x group interaction (line 140), normal contraction bias in controls, and the independent psychological (PSYCH) effect (line 132), which are individual tested effects rather than an overall replication verdict. For the explicitly tested accelerating overestimation (regression slope > 1) in the eating disorder group (line 87), the primary full-sample clinical analysis yielded a slope near 1 (beta = 0.95) contrasting with [17, 18], and only a post-hoc subgroup analysis excluding bulimia nervosa yielded results consistent with [17, 18] (beta = 1.18 > 1), leaving both beta = 1 and beta > 1 as competing possibilities (lines 116-129, 143). Under the codebook, mixed agreement across tested findings without an overriding whole-replication verdict is 'mixed'.

decisions.quote: In summary, the current study serves both as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17,18]. We aimed to replicate the differences in perceptual body image identified in these previous studies by improving the design in the following ways: a) ensuring a more accurate alignment of actual BMI ranges across participant groups, b) incorporating measures to control for sociocultural attitudes towards appearance, and c) implementing a refined psychophysical method for body size estimation that avoided emotionally loaded language in the responses.
decisions.location: Introduction > Emotional significance of deciding “larger/smaller than” another body, line 25
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding identify the record type as 'replication'. The authors collected new data from 133 women (100 healthy controls and 33 women with an eating disorder history) to re-test the perceptual and attitudinal body image findings of Cornelissen et al. [17, 18].

decisions.reason: The primary source ( Irvine et al., 2024, DOI `10.1371/journal.pone.0313619`) explicitly states in the Introduction (lines 150–152) that 'the current study serves both as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17,18]' and aims 'to replicate the differences in perceptual body image identified in these previous studies' (the group-by-actual-BMI interaction in self-estimated BMI and the independent contribution of psychological factors in women with a history of anorexia nervosa vs. healthy controls), and directly compares its empirical results to both [17] and [18] throughout the Results (lines 382–385) and Discussion (lines 517–536, 561–593). References [17] and [18] are two separate empirical articles: [17] is Cornelissen et al. (2015, Body Image, 13, 75–85, DOI `10.1016/j.bodyim.2015.01.001`, testing women with current anorexia spectrum disorder using standard 2D CGI stimuli), and [18] is Cornelissen, McCarty, Cornelissen, & Tovée (2017, Scientific Reports, 7, 15773, DOI `10.1038/s41598-017-15339-z`, testing women with current or past eating-disorder history using 3D avatars). The single shipped row (row 1858, originally listing Reference [20], Cornelissen et al., 2016, DOI `10.1111/bjhp.12185`) was already adjudicated to represent blind target 0 (Reference [17], Cornelissen et al., 2015, `10.1016/j.bodyim.2015.01.001`), leaving Reference [18] (Cornelissen et al., 2017, `10.1038/s41598-017-15339-z`) as a genuinely distinct and unrepresented missing replication target. Per review instructions when no paper outcome is requested, `outcome` is set to `cannot_be_determined`.
